content: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is a genetic disorder that is managed through dietary restriction of the amino acid phenylalanine. This dietary intervention is typically initiated during the neonatal period to prevent intellectual disability. However, the diet is highly restrictive and can be challenging to adhere to. There is ongoing debate about whether the diet can be relaxed or discontinued during adolescence or if it should be maintained throughout life. This review aims to address this issue. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of a low-phenylalanine diet started early in life for individuals with PKU. Additionally, it sought to assess the potential consequences of relaxing or discontinuing the diet on various outcomes, including intelligence, neuropsychological performance, mortality, growth, nutritional status, eating behavior, and quality of life. To gather evidence, the authors searched the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Trials Register, which includes references from extensive electronic database searches, manual searches of relevant journals, and conference proceedings. The most recent search of the Inborn Errors of Metabolism Trials Register was conducted on April 30, 2020. The review included all randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared a low-phenylalanine diet to a relaxed or discontinued dietary regimen in individuals with PKU. Two authors independently evaluated the eligibility and methodological quality of the studies and extracted the relevant data. Four studies involving a total of 251 participants were included in the review. The findings revealed few significant differences between the treatment and comparison groups for the outcomes of interest. Blood phenylalanine levels were significantly lower in participants who adhered to a low-phenylalanine diet compared to those on a less restricted diet. Specifically, the mean difference in blood phenylalanine levels at three months was -698.67 μmol/L (95% confidence interval: -869.44 to -527.89 μmol/L). Additionally, intelligence quotient (IQ) was significantly higher in participants who continued the diet compared to those who discontinued it. The mean difference in IQ after 12 months was 5.00 points (95% confidence interval: 0.40 to 9.60 points). However, this result was derived from a single study. The authors concluded that evidence from non-randomized studies supports the effectiveness of a low-phenylalanine diet in reducing blood phenylalanine levels and improving IQ and neuropsychological outcomes. However, no randomized controlled trials have assessed the effects of a low-phenylalanine diet compared to no dietary intervention from the time of diagnosis. Conducting such a study would be considered unethical given the existing evidence from non-randomized studies. Therefore, it is recommended that a low-phenylalanine diet be initiated at the time of diagnosis. There remains uncertainty regarding the optimal level of phenylalanine restriction and the appropriate timing, if any, for relaxing the diet. Addressing these questions would require randomized controlled trials. However, no new studies in this area are anticipated, and the authors do not plan to update this review.
